title: Functions, Graphs & Logarithms
summary: Function notation, graphs, modulus and logarithms — the algebra engine room of management exams. Banking and SSC papers meet it mainly in Tier 2 and higher-level sets, where 1–2 clean, formula-driven questions reward anyone who knows the standard moves.

subtopics.title: Functions, domain & range
subtopics.concept: A function is a machine: one input in, exactly one output out. The domain lists the inputs the machine accepts, and the range lists the outputs it can actually produce.

formulas.name: Domain: denominator
formulas.note: Reject every input that makes the bottom zero.

formulas.name: Domain: square root
formulas.note: The inside of a root stays on the non-negative side.

formulas.name: Range of a quadratic
formulas.note: Complete the square; $k$ is the floor or the ceiling.

formulas.name: Vertex input
formulas.note: Substitute back to get the minimum or maximum value.

formulas.name: Even / odd test
formulas.note: Replace $x$ by $-x$ and simplify fully before deciding.

tricks.title: Hunt the two troublemakers
tricks.body: For a domain, only two things can go wrong: a zero bottom or a negative root. Scan the rule for $\div$ and $\sqrt{}$, write the condition, solve.

steps: Bottom is $x - 7$; it must not be zero.

tricks.title: Complete the square for range
tricks.body: Write $ax^2 + bx + c$ as $a(x - h)^2 + k$. The square cannot go below $0$, so $k$ is the smallest (or largest) output.

example.q: Find the minimum value of $f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 7$.

tricks.title: Test $f(-1)$ for even / odd
tricks.body: Compute $f(-1)$ and compare with $f(1)$ and $-f(1)$. Equal means even, opposite means odd. Always confirm with the full rule $f(-x)$.

example.q: Is $f(x) = x^3 - x$ even, odd or neither?

mistakes: Treating $x = 0$ as always forbidden — only a denominator equal to zero is forbidden, not the input zero itself.
Giving the domain of $\sqrt{x-4}$ as all real numbers — the inside must stay $\ge 0$, so $x \ge 4$.
Swapping domain and range — domain is the set of inputs, range is the set of outputs.
For $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x-2}}$, writing $x \ge 2$ — the bottom cannot be zero, so $x > 2$ strictly.
Testing even/odd at a single value and concluding without checking the rule $f(-x)$ for all $x$.
Judging even/odd from the powers alone — $x^2 + 1$ is even and $x^3 + 1$ is neither; only the test with $f(-x)$ decides.
subtopics.notes:
### A function is a machine
Think of a currency-exchange counter. You hand over a number, the machine applies one fixed rule, and hands back exactly one number. That is a function.

We write $f(x) = 2x + 3$. Here $f$ is the rule, $x$ is the input, and $f(x)$ is the output.

Feed in $x = 4$: $f(4) = 2(4) + 3 = 11$.

> **Rule:** One input must give exactly one output. If some input gives two different outputs, it is not a function.

### Checking a relation is a function
Take the pairs $(1, 2)$, $(2, 5)$, $(1, 7)$. The input $1$ gives two outputs, $2$ and $7$. Not a function.

Now $(1, 2)$, $(2, 5)$, $(3, 5)$. Inputs $2$ and $3$ share the output $5$ — that is allowed. Two inputs may share one output; one input may not split into two outputs.

On a graph this becomes the vertical line test: a vertical line must cut the curve at most once.

### Domain: which inputs are allowed
The domain is the set of inputs the machine accepts. Two things break a machine:

1. Division by zero. In $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{x-3}$, the input $x = 3$ gives $\dfrac{1}{0}$. Reject it. Domain: all real numbers except $3$.
2. Square roots of negatives. In $f(x) = \sqrt{x-5}$, the input must keep $x - 5 \ge 0$, so $x \ge 5$.

Polynomials like $x^2 + 3x$ carry no such traps. Every real number is allowed.

> **Watch:** For $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x-3}}$ both traps act together. The root needs $x - 3 \ge 0$ and the bottom cannot be zero, so $x > 3$ strictly.

Worked: domain of $\dfrac{x+1}{x^2 - 5x + 6}$. Factor the bottom: $(x-2)(x-3)$. Reject $x = 2$ and $x = 3$.

### Range: which outputs can come out
The range is the set of outputs the machine can actually produce.

A straight line like $f(x) = 2x + 5$ climbs forever in both directions. It can output every real number.

A parabola has a floor or a ceiling. Complete the square to find it:

$$f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 7 = (x-2)^2 + 3$$

A square is never negative, so the smallest output is $3$, reached at $x = 2$. Range: $f(x) \ge 3$.

If the $x^2$ term carries a minus sign, the parabola opens down. Then the vertex value is the maximum.

> **Tip:** For $a(x-h)^2 + k$, the range is $[k, \infty)$ when $a > 0$ and $(-\infty, k]$ when $a < 0$.

### Even and odd functions
Replace $x$ by $-x$ and simplify.

- Same result: $f(-x) = f(x)$ — even. The graph mirrors in the $y$-axis. Example: $x^4 + x^2$ stays itself.
- Sign flips: $f(-x) = -f(x)$ — odd. The graph looks the same after a half turn. Example: $x^3 + x$ flips sign cleanly.
- Neither: $f(x) = x + 1$ gives $-x + 1$, which is neither $f(x)$ nor $-f(x)$.

> **Note:** Test the rule, not the powers. $x^2 + 1$ is even though $1$ is an odd number; $x^3 + 1$ is neither.

### Reading the question
Exams ask value, domain, range and symmetry as four separate question types.

- "For which values is $f$ defined?" — hunt denominators and roots first.
- "The minimum value of $f(x)$" — complete the square.
- "Find $k$ given the minimum" — vertex form, then compare.
- "Even, odd or neither" — compute $f(-x)$ fully before deciding.

Write the restriction first, then answer. That order catches almost every domain error.

patterns.name: Find the value of a function
patterns.howToSpot: A rule like $f(x) = 3x - 4$ is given and $f(5)$ or $f(a) + f(b)$ is asked.
steps: Replace every $x$ by the given number, in brackets.
For $f(a) + f(b)$, evaluate each part separately.
patterns.why: A function value is just the output of the rule at that input, so substitution is the whole method.

patterns.name: Domain of a rational function
patterns.howToSpot: The rule is a fraction. 'For what values of $x$ is $f$ defined?' is asked.
steps: Set the bottom equal to zero.
State the domain as all reals except those values.
For a quadratic bottom, factor or use the formula.
patterns.why: Division by zero is undefined, so exactly the zeros of the bottom drop out of the domain.

patterns.name: Domain with a square root
patterns.howToSpot: The rule contains $\sqrt{\;}$ of an expression in $x$, alone or under a fraction.
steps: Keep the inside of the root $\ge 0$.
If the root sits in a denominator, make it strict: $> 0$.
Combine both conditions when both appear.
patterns.why: Square roots of negative numbers are not real, so the inside must stay on the non-negative side.

patterns.name: Range of a linear function
patterns.howToSpot: $f(x) = ax + b$ with $a \ne 0$, and the set of possible outputs is asked.
steps: Check the slope $a$ is not zero.
A non-horizontal line climbs or falls forever.
Conclude the range is all real numbers.
patterns.why: A slanted line keeps rising or falling without end, so no output value is missed.

steps: As $x$ runs over all reals, $2x + 5$ also runs over all reals.

patterns.name: Range or minimum of a quadratic
patterns.howToSpot: $ax^2 + bx + c$ is given and its minimum (or maximum) value, or the full range, is asked.
steps: Note the sign of $a$: $a > 0$ gives a minimum.
Substitute the vertex input back into $f$.
Write the range from the vertex value.
patterns.why: The parabola turns around at its vertex, so the vertex value bounds the range on one side.

patterns.name: Even, odd or neither
patterns.howToSpot: '$f(x) = \ldots$ is:' with options even / odd / neither. Symmetry is asked without drawing.
patterns.why: Even means the rule is blind to the sign of $x$; odd means the output flips sign with the input.

revision: Function: one input gives exactly one output.
Line $ax + b$, $a \ne 0$: range is all real numbers.
Quadratic $a(x-h)^2 + k$: least or greatest value is $k$.

subtopics.title: Composite & inverse functions
subtopics.concept: A composite feeds one function's output into another: $f(g(x))$. An inverse runs a function backwards, turning each output into the input it came from.

formulas.name: Sum-type equation
formulas.tex: f(x+y) = f(x) + f(y),\ f(1) = k \Rightarrow f(x) = kx

formulas.name: Product-type equation
formulas.tex: f(x+y) = f(x)f(y),\ f(1) = k \Rightarrow f(x) = k^x

tricks.title: Work inside out
tricks.body: In $f(g(a))$, compute $g(a)$ first, box it, then feed that number into $f$. Two tiny calculations, no algebra.

tricks.title: Swap-and-solve for inverses
tricks.body: Write $y = f(x)$, swap $x$ and $y$, solve for $y$. Works for every invertible rule, including fractions.

tricks.title: Climb from the given value
tricks.body: Functional equations reward stepping: use $x = y = 1$ to get $f(2)$, then $f(2)$ and $f(1)$ for $f(3)$, and so on.

mistakes: Computing $f(g(x))$ as $g(f(x))$ — the order matters; in $f \circ g$ the inner rule $g$ acts first.
Treating $f^{-1}(x)$ as $1/f(x)$ — the $-1$ means undo, not divide.
Swapping $x$ and $y$ but not solving for $y$ — the inverse must end as '$y =$ rule in $x$'.
Assuming every function has an inverse — $x^2$ sends $2$ and $-2$ to the same output, so it cannot be undone on all reals.
In $f(x+y) = f(x) + f(y)$, guessing $f(x) = x$ without using the given $f(1)$ — the given value fixes the multiple.
For a shifted rule like $f(x+y) = f(x) + f(y) + 3$, forgetting the extra $+3$ at every step.
subtopics.notes:
### Two machines in a line
A tiffin service: the first machine packs rice, the second adds a sweet. Feed $x$ through $g$ first, then push the result through $f$. The combined rule is the composite, written $f(g(x))$ or $f \circ g$.

Take $f(x) = x + 1$ and $g(x) = 2x$.

$f(g(3))$: $g(3) = 6$, then $f(6) = 7$.

> **Rule:** In $f(g(x))$, always work from the inside out. $g$ acts first, $f$ acts on what comes out.

### Order matters
Swap the machines and watch the answer change.

$g(f(3))$: $f(3) = 4$, then $g(4) = 8$.

So $f(g(3)) = 7$ but $g(f(3)) = 8$. In general the two composites differ. Never run $f$ first unless the question says $g \circ f$.

Building the full rule is plain substitution. With $f(x) = x + 3$ and $g(x) = 2x$:

$$f(g(x)) = f(2x) = 2x + 3$$

The reverse: $g(f(x)) = 2(x + 3) = 2x + 6$. Same parts, different result.

### The inverse machine
The inverse $f^{-1}$ runs the machine backwards: output in, original input out.

If $f(x) = 3x - 2$, then $f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{x+2}{3}$.

Find it by swap-and-solve:

1. Write $y = 3x - 2$.
2. Swap: $x = 3y - 2$.
3. Solve for $y$: $y = \dfrac{x+2}{3}$.

Check: $f(2) = 4$, then $f^{-1}(4) = 2$. Back where we started.

> **Watch:** $f^{-1}(x)$ is not $\dfrac{1}{f(x)}$. The $-1$ means "undo", never "divide by".

### When an inverse exists
Undoing needs each output to point back to exactly one input.

$f(x) = x^2$ fails: $2$ and $-2$ both give $4$, so $4$ cannot choose a way back. Restrict to $x \ge 0$ and it works: $f^{-1}(x) = \sqrt{x}$.

Fractional linear functions always pass. For $f(x) = \dfrac{ax+b}{cx+d}$, swap-and-solve gives

$$f^{-1}(x) = \frac{b - dx}{cx - a}$$

> **Tip:** When $d = -a$, the function is its own inverse. Check: $f(x) = \dfrac{3x+1}{x-3}$ undoes itself, so $f^{-1}(t) = f(t)$ for every $t$.

### Functional equations
The question gives a rule connecting values of $f$ and asks for one value. Feed small numbers and climb.

Take $f(x+y) = f(x) + f(y)$ with $f(1) = 5$. Each step adds $5$: $f(2) = 10$, $f(3) = 15$, so $f(7) = 35$. In general $f(x) = 5x$.

The product version $f(x+y) = f(x) \cdot f(y)$ with $f(1) = 3$ multiplies at every step: $f(2) = 9$, $f(3) = 27$, $f(4) = 81$. Such a function is $f(x) = 3^x$.

A shifted rule needs the same climbing, one step at a time. For $f(x+y) = f(x) + f(y) + 3$ with $f(1) = 2$:

$f(2) = 2 + 2 + 3 = 7$, then $f(3) = f(2) + f(1) + 3 = 12$.

> **Note:** In every functional equation, build outward from the given value using the given rule. Two or three steps almost always reach the asked value.

### Reading the question
- "Find $f(g(2))$" — evaluate the inside rule first.
- "Find $f^{-1}(3)$" — swap-and-solve, or substitute into the inverse formula.
- "Is $f^{-1}$ possible?" — look for two inputs sharing one output.
- "$f(x+y) = \ldots$, find $f(10)$" — iterate from $f(1)$; the steps repeat.

patterns.name: Composite at a point
patterns.howToSpot: Two rules $f$ and $g$ are given and $f(g(a))$ or $g(f(a))$ is asked for a number $a$.
steps: Spot the inner function (the one next to $a$).
Feed the result into the outer rule.
Check which composition the question names.
patterns.why: A composite is two substitutions done one after another, so point-wise evaluation is fastest.

patterns.name: Build or compare the composite rule
patterns.howToSpot: 'Find $f(g(x))$' as a rule, or the difference $f(g(x)) - g(f(x))$ is asked.
patterns.formula: f(g(x)) = \text{(outer rule with inner rule substituted)}
steps: Substitute the inner rule into the outer one.
Build the reverse composite too if asked.
Subtract or compare as the question says.
patterns.why: Composition is substitution of one whole rule into the other, so algebra finishes it.

patterns.name: Find the inverse function
patterns.howToSpot: $f(x)$ is given and $f^{-1}(x)$ is asked — often for the fractional linear shape $\dfrac{ax+b}{cx+d}$.
patterns.why: The inverse swaps the roles of input and output, so interchanging the letters and re-solving does the job.

patterns.name: Self-inverse and inverse values
patterns.howToSpot: $f(x) = \dfrac{ax+b}{x-a}$ (bottom constant is minus the top coefficient of $x$), or $f^{-1}(t)$ is asked for one number $t$.
patterns.why: A self-inverse function undoes itself, so the inverse value equals the function value.

patterns.name: Functional equation of sum type
patterns.howToSpot: A rule like $f(x+y) = f(x) + f(y)$ (possibly with a constant added) and one value such as $f(1)$ are given.
patterns.formula: f(x+y) = f(x) + f(y),\ f(1) = k \Rightarrow f(x) = kx
steps: Climb one step at a time.
For the shifted rule, add the constant at every step.
State the general form if asked.
patterns.why: The rule tells how outputs combine, so known small values generate all the others.

example.q: If $f(x+y) = f(x) + f(y) + 3$ for all $x, y$ and $f(1) = 2$, find $f(3)$.

patterns.name: Functional equation of product type
patterns.howToSpot: A rule like $f(x+y) = f(x) \cdot f(y)$ and a value such as $f(1) = 3$ or $f(3) = 8$ are given.
patterns.formula: f(x+y) = f(x)f(y),\ f(1) = k \Rightarrow f(x) = k^x
steps: Each extra unit multiplies once more.
$f(n)$ equals the given value to the power $n$ (or a matching power).
Use powers of powers for big jumps.
patterns.why: The rule multiplies outputs as inputs add, which is exactly how powers behave.

revision: Sum type: $f(x) = kx$. Product type: $f(x) = k^x$.
No inverse when two inputs share one output.

subtopics.title: Graphs & transformations
subtopics.concept: Every function has a picture. Rules like $f(x) + k$, $f(x - a)$, $-f(x)$ and $|f(x)|$ slide, flip or fold that picture in fixed ways, and the vertex of a parabola gives its peak or valley.

formulas.name: Reflections
formulas.note: First flips over the $x$-axis, second over the $y$-axis.

formulas.name: Modulus graph
formulas.note: The part below the axis is reflected up.

tricks.title: Vertex in one line
tricks.body: For $ax^2 + bx + c$, the turning input is $-b/2a$. Substitute it back for the peak or valley value. Check the sign of $a$ first.

tricks.title: Inside moves opposite
tricks.body: For shifts, look at where the rule sits: inside the bracket means the move is opposite to the sign; outside means the move is as written.

tricks.title: Count crossings, not algebra
tricks.body: For 'how many solutions', sketch the V or parabola roughly and count crossings with the horizontal line. No solving needed.

steps: V with corner at $x = -2$, opening up.

mistakes: Reading $f(x + 3)$ as a shift right — inside changes work in reverse: $f(x+3)$ is $3$ left.
Taking $y = f(x) + 2$ down — an outside $+k$ lifts the picture up.
For $y = |f(x)|$, mirroring the above-axis part too — only the part below the axis folds up.
Calling the vertex a minimum for every quadratic — if $a < 0$ the parabola opens down and the vertex is a maximum.
Reflecting the wrong coordinate: $y = -f(x)$ flips $y$-values, $y = f(-x)$ flips $x$-values.
Answering '2 solutions' for $|x - a| = 0$ — at the corner the V meets the line once, not twice.
subtopics.notes:
### A graph is a picture of the rule
Every point on the curve $y = f(x)$ says: at input $x$, the output is $f(x)$.

For $f(x) = 2x + 1$ the points $(0, 1)$, $(1, 3)$, $(2, 5)$ line up into a straight line.

Graph questions are scoring. The paper shows a shifted parabola or a V shape and asks where it peaks, where it cuts an axis, or how many times it crosses a line.

### Sliding up and down
Adding outside the bracket lifts or lowers the whole picture.

$y = f(x) + 3$ moves every point up by $3$. $y = f(x) - 2$ drops it by $2$.

The parabola $y = x^2$ has its lowest point at $(0, 0)$. So $y = x^2 + 4$ has its lowest point at $(0, 4)$.

> **Rule:** Changes made outside the rule (added after $f$) move the picture up or down, exactly as written.

### Sliding left and right
Changes inside the bracket work in reverse.

$y = f(x - 2)$ moves the picture $2$ units right. $y = f(x + 3)$ moves it $3$ units left.

Why backwards? At $x = 2$, the rule $f(x-2)$ computes $f(0)$ — the old picture starts where the new zero sits.

The parabola $y = (x-2)^2$ has its vertex at $x = 2$: the old vertex at $0$ has walked to $2$.

> **Watch:** Inside changes are opposite. $(x - a)$ shifts right, $(x + a)$ shifts left. Under pressure, this is the one students flip.

### Flips and mirrors
- $y = -f(x)$: outputs multiplied by $-1$. The picture flips over the $x$-axis — a water image. Point $(3, -2)$ becomes $(3, 2)$.
- $y = f(-x)$: inputs replaced by their negatives. The picture flips over the $y$-axis — a mirror image. Point $(2, 5)$ becomes $(-2, 5)$.

The point itself tells you the answer: flip the sign of the $y$ for the first, flip the sign of the $x$ for the second.

### The modulus folds the graph up
$y = |f(x)|$ keeps everything on or above the axis. Outputs below zero are reflected up; the rest stays put.

$y = |x - 3|$ is a V with its corner at $(3, 0)$ and arms climbing at $45^\circ$. It cuts the $y$-axis where $|0 - 3| = 3$, at $(0, 3)$.

Only the below-axis part folds. The above-axis part never changes.

> **Tip:** For $y = |x - a|$, draw a V with corner at $(a, 0)$. Read crossings straight off the picture.

### The parabola and its vertex
For $f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c$:

- $a > 0$: opens up, vertex is the minimum.
- $a < 0$: opens down, vertex is the maximum.
- Vertex input: $x = -\dfrac{b}{2a}$.

Worked: $f(x) = -2x^2 + 12x - 11$. Here $a = -2 < 0$, so a maximum exists. $x = -\dfrac{12}{-4} = 3$. Then $f(3) = -18 + 36 - 11 = 7$. Maximum value $7$.

Where the graph meets the $x$-axis, put $f(x) = 0$. For $(x-1)^2 - 4 = 0$: $(x-1)^2 = 4$, so $x = 3$ or $x = -1$.

> **Example:** $f(x) = x^2 - 6x + 8$ has vertex at $x = 3$ and cuts the axis where $(x-2)(x-3) = 0$, at $x = 2$ and $x = 3$.

### Counting solutions from a picture
"How many solutions?" means "how many times do the two pictures cross?"

$|2x - 5| = 3$: the V with corner at $x = 2.5$ meets the flat line $y = 3$ twice. Answer: $2$ solutions.

A horizontal line above a V's corner cuts it twice; exactly at the corner, once; below the corner, never.

> **Rule:** Rough-sketch the V or parabola with its corner and one point on each arm. Counting crossings beats algebra when only the number of solutions is asked.

patterns.name: Vertex: maximum or minimum value
patterns.howToSpot: A quadratic is given and 'the maximum/minimum value of $f(x)$' or the input where it occurs is asked.
steps: Check the sign of $a$ for min or max.
State both the input and the value if asked.
patterns.why: The parabola turns around at its vertex, so the vertex carries the peak or the valley.

example.q: Find the minimum value of $f(x) = x^2 - 8x + 17$.

patterns.name: Shift a graph
patterns.howToSpot: '$y = f(x)$ is shifted...' or a new rule like $f(x - 3) + 1$ is given and the movement is asked.
steps: Look for changes inside the bracket: they move opposite.
Look for changes outside: they move as written.
patterns.why: Inputs feed the rule from inside, so an inside change delays or advances the picture — the reverse of its sign.

patterns.name: Graph of a modulus
patterns.howToSpot: A rule with $|\;|$, or 'the graph of $y = |x - a|$...' with an axis crossing asked.
patterns.formula: |x - a| = \begin{cases} x - a, & x \ge a \\ a - x, & x < a \end{cases}
steps: For $|f(x)|$, fold the below-axis part up.
Read axis crossings from the sketch.
patterns.why: A modulus erases negative signs, so the picture is whatever remains above the axis.

patterns.name: Count solutions from the picture
patterns.howToSpot: 'How many solutions does ... have?' — usually a modulus or parabola against a constant.
steps: Sketch the modulus V or the parabola roughly.
Draw the horizontal line on the other side.
patterns.why: Each crossing is one solution, so a rough sketch answers a counting question without solving.

steps: Line $y = 3$ is above the corner value $0$.

patterns.name: Reflect a graph or a point
patterns.howToSpot: '$(a, b)$ lies on $y = f(x)$. Which point lies on $y = -f(x)$ or $y = f(-x)$?'
patterns.formula: y = -f(x): (a, b) \to (a, -b); \quad y = f(-x): (a, b) \to (-a, b)
steps: Identify which rule changed: outside minus flips outputs.
Change the sign of the matching coordinate.
patterns.why: Multiplying outputs by $-1$ reflects over the $x$-axis; negating inputs reflects over the $y$-axis.

example.q: $(3, -2)$ lies on $y = f(x)$. Which point lies on $y = -f(x)$?

patterns.name: Where a graph meets the axes
patterns.howToSpot: 'The graph of ... cuts the x-axis at' — find roots, or the y-axis crossing.
patterns.why: Crossings are exactly the points where one coordinate is zero, so one substitution does it.

revision: Inside changes work opposite to their sign.
Axis crossings: put the other coordinate equal to $0$.

subtopics.title: Logarithms
subtopics.concept: A logarithm asks 'what power?'. $\log_2 32 = 5$ because $2^5 = 32$. Three laws handle products, quotients and powers, and the base decides how inequalities behave.

formulas.name: Product / quotient laws
formulas.note: Multiplication becomes addition; division becomes subtraction.

formulas.name: Change of base
formulas.note: Any common base works; base 10 is standard.

formulas.name: Special values
formulas.note: Log of 1 is 0; log of the base is 1; base and log cancel.

tricks.title: Translate to power language
tricks.body: Read every log aloud as 'base to the what gives this?'. Then match powers of the base. No formula needed for direct values.

tricks.title: Fraction or root arguments: use negative and fractional powers
tricks.body: $1/8$ is $2^{-3}$, $27$ is $3^3$, $\sqrt{9}$ is $9^{1/2}$. Write both sides with the same base and the answer falls out.

tricks.title: Split products, pop powers
tricks.body: Seeing a product inside a log, split it. Seeing a power, bring it out front. Known values such as $\log 2 = 0.3010$ then finish the job.

mistakes: Reading $\log_2 8$ as $8 \div 2$ — a log asks for the power: $2^3 = 8$, so the answer is $3$.
Splitting $\log_a(m + n)$ into $\log_a m + \log_a n$ — the laws work on products and quotients, never sums.
Forgetting the base condition in inequalities — with base $\dfrac{1}{2}$ the sign flips.
Ignoring the domain: $\log(x - 2)$ needs $x > 2$, so a root making the argument zero or negative must be rejected.
Writing change of base upside down — $\log_a b = \dfrac{\log b}{\log a}$, both logs of the same side stay together.
Assuming $\log 100 = 2$ in every base — that is a base-10 fact; $\log_2 100$ is about $6.64$.
subtopics.notes:
### A log asks: what power?
A logarithm answers one question: this base, raised to what power, gives that number?

$2$ to the what gives $32$? Count the doublings: $2, 4, 8, 16, 32$ — five. So $\log_2 32 = 5$.

The three players: $2$ is the base, $32$ is the argument, $5$ is the answer.

Read $\log_5 125$ as "$5$ to the what is $125$?" The answer is $3$.

### The definition is the master key
$$\log_a b = x \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad a^x = b$$

Any log question can be rewritten as a power question. Three small ones:

- $\log_3 81$: $3^4 = 81$, so the answer is $4$.
- $\log_5 \dfrac{1}{25}$: $5^{-2} = \dfrac{1}{25}$, so the answer is $-2$.
- $\log_7 1$: any power $0$ gives $1$, so the answer is $0$.

Conditions: the base is positive and not $1$; the argument must be positive. Logs of zero or negatives do not exist.

> **Rule:** Stuck on any log — convert it to "$a^x = b$" and match the powers.

### Three laws, one idea
Logs turn multiplication into addition, division into subtraction, and powers into multiples.

- $\log_a(mn) = \log_a m + \log_a n$ — a product becomes a sum.
- $\log_a \dfrac{m}{n} = \log_a m - \log_a n$ — a quotient becomes a difference.
- $\log_a m^p = p \log_a m$ — the power pops out front.

Worked: $\log_{10} 4 + \log_{10} 25 = \log_{10}(4 \times 25) = \log_{10} 100 = 2$.

And $\log_{10} 8 = \log_{10} 2^3 = 3\log_{10} 2$. With $\log_{10} 2 = 0.3010$, this is $0.9030$.

> **Watch:** The laws work on products and quotients, never on sums. $\log(m + n)$ is not $\log m + \log n$.

### Change of base
To evaluate a log in an awkward base, divide two logs in a friendly base:

$$\log_a b = \frac{\log_{10} b}{\log_{10} a}$$

Worked: $\log_2 5 = \dfrac{\log 5}{\log 2} = \dfrac{0.6990}{0.3010} \approx 2.32$.

The same idea links related bases. Since $4 = 2^2$:

$$\log_4 x = \frac{1}{2}\log_2 x$$

So $\log_2 x + \log_4 x = \dfrac{3}{2}\log_2 x$. If that equals $3$, then $\log_2 x = 2$ and $x = 4$.

One identity more: $a^{\log_a b} = b$. Base and log cancel, leaving the argument: $5^{\log_5 9} = 9$.

### Log equations and the domain check
Same base on both sides: equate the powers.

$\log_2(x - 1) = 5$ means $x - 1 = 2^5 = 32$, so $x = 33$.

Products need one extra step. Solve $\log_{10} x + \log_{10}(x - 3) = 1$:

1. Combine: $\log_{10}\big(x(x-3)\big) = 1$.
2. So $x(x - 3) = 10$, giving $x^2 - 3x - 10 = 0$.
3. Roots: $x = 5$ and $x = -2$.
4. Domain check: $x = -2$ makes $\log_{10}(-2)$ impossible. Reject it.

Answer: $x = 5$ only. This rejection is exactly where exam setters plant a trap option.

> **Watch:** After solving a log equation, test every root in the original question. Arguments must stay positive.

### Inequalities: the base rule
Base greater than $1$: the log climbs, so the inequality sign stays.

$\log_2 x < 4$ gives $0 < x < 16$ — below by the power, and $x$ must stay positive.

Base between $0$ and $1$: the log falls as $x$ grows, so the sign flips.

$\log_{1/2} x > 3$: compare with the power $\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^3 = \dfrac{1}{8}$. Bigger log now means smaller argument: $0 < x < \dfrac{1}{8}$.

> **Rule:** A small base ($0 < a < 1$) reverses the inequality. Check with one number: $\log_{1/2} \dfrac{1}{16} = 4 > 3$, and $\dfrac{1}{16} < \dfrac{1}{8}$. Consistent.

Write the argument as a power of the base.

Combine into one log, or split a big one.

For related bases, use $\log_{a^k} x = \frac{1}{k}\log_a x$.

Reject roots that break the domain.

Write the answer as one interval.

Cancel the pair: the argument remains.

Base below 1 flips the inequality; always keep $x > 0$.

subtopics.title: Modulus & equations
subtopics.concept: The modulus $|x|$ is a distance, so it is never negative. Equations split into two cases, inequalities give a band or two arms, and exponential equations fall to matching bases.

formulas.name: Exponential match
formulas.note: Write both sides with the same base first.

tricks.title: Think distance, not cases
tricks.body: $|x - 3| = 2$ asks for points at distance $2$ from $3$. Walk $2$ left and $2$ right: $x = 1$ and $x = 5$. No case work.

tricks.title: Band or arms — one glance
tricks.body: For $|x - a| < d$ the answer sits between $a - d$ and $a + d$. For $> d$ it sits outside those two numbers.

tricks.title: Subtract the pins for the minimum
tricks.body: The least value of $|x - a| + |x - b|$ is the gap between the pins. One subtraction, done.

mistakes: Solving $|x| = -4$ and writing $x = \pm 4$ — a modulus is never negative, so there is no solution.
Splitting $|x - 2| < 5$ as $x < 7$ only — the other side gives $x > -3$ too.
Writing $-a < x < a$ for $|x| > a$ — that is the band for '<'; the sign '>' gives two arms outside.
Accepting a case root without checking it in the original equation — fake roots appear when the right side contains $x$.
Putting the minimum of $|x-a| + |x-b|$ only at $x = a$ — every point between the pins gives the same minimum.
Solving $2^{x+1} = 8$ as $x + 1 = 8$ — first write $8 = 2^3$, then equate powers: $x + 1 = 3$.
subtopics.notes:
### Modulus means distance
$|x|$ is the distance of $x$ from $0$. Distance is never negative, so $|-7| = 7$ and $|7| = 7$.

$|x - 3|$ is the distance of $x$ from $3$. The point $x = 5$ sits at distance $2$, and so does $x = 1$: both give $|x - 3| = 2$.

Distance thinking solves modulus questions faster than algebra. Ask: which points sit at this distance from this number?

> **Rule:** $|x - a| = d$ means $x$ sits at distance $d$ from $a$ — the two points $a + d$ and $a - d$.

### Equations: split into two cases
The inside of a modulus is either positive or negative. Solve both ways.

Solve $|2x - 3| = 5$:

1. Case one: $2x - 3 = 5$, so $x = 4$.
2. Case two: $2x - 3 = -5$, so $x = -1$.
3. Both are valid: $x = 4$ or $x = -1$.

Or use distance: $|x - 2| = 5$ asks for points at distance $5$ from $2$, namely $7$ and $-3$.

$|x| = -4$ has no solution — no distance is negative.

### Inequalities: inside or outside
$|x - a| < d$ keeps $x$ within distance $d$ of $a$ — one band.

$|x - 3| < 4$ gives $-1 < x < 7$.

$|x - a| > d$ pushes $x$ outside the band — two arms.

$|2x - 1| \ge 5$: the quantity $2x - 1$ sits at least $5$ from zero, so $2x - 1 \ge 5$ or $2x - 1 \le -5$. That gives $x \ge 3$ or $x \le -2$.

> **Watch:** "<" gives one interval, ">" gives two arms. Mixing them up is the most common modulus error in the paper.

### Sum of two distances
$|x - a| + |x - b|$ adds the distances from $x$ to two fixed pins $a$ and $b$.

Walk between the pins: each step moves you closer to one pin and further from the other by the same amount, so the total stays fixed inside.

$$\text{minimum of } |x-a| + |x-b| = |a - b|$$

Worked: the minimum of $|x - 4| + |x + 2|$ is the gap between the pins $4$ and $-2$, which is $6$. Every $x$ from $-2$ to $4$ achieves it.

Outside the pins the total grows: at $x = 10$ it is already $18$.

> **Tip:** For the minimum of $|x - a| + |x - b|$, just subtract the pins. Any $x$ between them achieves it.

### The validity check
When a modulus equals an expression containing $x$, a case solution can be fake. Test each root in the original equation.

Solve $|x - 3| = 2x - 5$:

1. Case $x \ge 3$: $x - 3 = 2x - 5$ gives $x = 2$. But $2 < 3$ — the root breaks its own case. Reject.
2. Case $x < 3$: $3 - x = 2x - 5$ gives $3x = 8$, so $x = \dfrac{8}{3}$.
3. Check: $\left|\dfrac{8}{3} - 3\right| = \dfrac{1}{3}$ and $2 \cdot \dfrac{8}{3} - 5 = \dfrac{1}{3}$. Valid.

Answer: $x = \dfrac{8}{3}$ alone. The right side $2x - 5$ must be non-negative for any solution, and $x = 2$ made it negative.

### Exponential equations
Match the bases, then equate the powers.

$2^x = 64$: since $64 = 2^6$, $x = 6$.

$3^{x+2} = 27$: since $27 = 3^3$, $x + 2 = 3$ and $x = 1$.

Products on one side add powers. $2^x \cdot 2^{x+1} = 32$ becomes $2^{2x+1} = 2^5$, so $2x + 1 = 5$ and $x = 2$.

When no power matches, take logs: $3^x = 20$ gives $x = \dfrac{\log 20}{\log 3}$.

> **Note:** Every exponential equation is a log equation with the base matched first. Logs step in only when the bases refuse to match.

patterns.name: Solve |expression| = number
patterns.howToSpot: An equation like $|2x - 3| = 5$ or $|x - 2| = 5$ with two solutions expected.
steps: Write the two cases: inside $= +d$ and $= -d$.
Or use distance: $a + d$ and $a - d$.
patterns.why: The inside of a modulus can be positive or negative, so both sign choices are candidates.

patterns.name: Modulus inequality: inside the band
patterns.howToSpot: $|x - a| < d$ or $\le d$ — one interval is the answer.
patterns.formula: |x - a| < d \Rightarrow a - d < x < a + d
steps: Keep strict or loose signs as given.
patterns.why: Staying within distance $d$ of $a$ means living inside the band of radius $d$.

patterns.name: Modulus inequality: outside the band
patterns.howToSpot: $|x - a| > d$ or $\ge d$ — two separate arms are the answer.
patterns.formula: |x - a| > d \Rightarrow x < a - d \text{ or } x > a + d
steps: Split into the two cases $\ge d$ and $\le -d$ inside.
patterns.why: Being further than $d$ from $a$ leaves only the two outer regions of the line.

patterns.name: Minimum of |x−a| + |x−b|
patterns.howToSpot: 'The minimum value of $|x - a| + |x - b|$' with two fixed numbers $a$ and $b$.
steps: State that any $x$ between them achieves it.
Check one inside value if unsure.
patterns.why: Between the pins, one distance grows exactly as the other shrinks, so the sum cannot drop below the gap.

patterns.name: Equations needing a validity check
patterns.howToSpot: A modulus equals an expression with $x$, like $|x - 3| = 2x - 5$. One case may fail.
steps: Split into the two sign cases.
Check each root in the original equation.
Reject roots that make the non-modulus side negative or break the case.
patterns.why: A modulus is non-negative, so the other side must be too — some algebraic roots break that.

patterns.name: Exponential equation by matching bases
patterns.howToSpot: Powers like $2^x = 64$ or $3^{x+2} = 27$ — both sides can share one base.
steps: Write both sides as powers of the same base.
patterns.why: Equal powers of the same base force equal exponents.

revision: $|x - a| = d$: two answers, $a + d$ and $a - d$.
$|x - a| < d$: one band; $|x - a| > d$: two arms.
$\min(|x-a| + |x-b|) = |a - b|$, true for all $x$ between the pins.
Check every root when a modulus equals an expression in $x$.
$a^{f(x)} = a^{g(x)}$ gives $f(x) = g(x)$ after matching bases.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A rule like $f(x) = x^2 + 2x$ is given and a value such as $f(3)$ is asked.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Substitute the number into the rule.
Simplify in one careful line.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Domain of a rational or root function
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'For what values of $x$ is $f$ defined?' — the rule has a denominator or a root.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Reject inputs that make the denominator zero.
Keep the inside of every root non-negative.

example.solution:
$x^2 - 5x + 6 = (x-2)(x-3)$
Reject $x = 2$ and $x = 3$: domain is all reals except **2 and 3**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Two rules $f$ and $g$ are given; $f(g(a))$ is asked for a number.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Evaluate the inner rule first.
Feed the result into the outer rule.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Inverse of a fractional linear function
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: $f(x) = \dfrac{ax+b}{cx+d}$ is given and $f^{-1}(x)$ or $f^{-1}(t)$ is asked.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Use $f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{b-dx}{cx-a}$, or swap and solve.
For $f^{-1}(t)$ with $d = -a$, just compute $f(t)$.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: $f(x+y) = f(x) + f(y)$ style with one value like $f(1)$ given.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Climb one unit step at a time from the given value.
Sum type adds; product type multiplies.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Maximum or minimum of a quadratic via the vertex
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Find the maximum/minimum value of $ax^2 + bx + c$' — or the input where it occurs.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Vertex at $x = -b/2a$.
$a > 0$ gives a minimum, $a < 0$ a maximum.
Substitute back for the value.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A log value is asked directly, or logs of products and powers must be combined.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Convert to power language.
Split products into sums; pop powers out front.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Log equation with a rejected root
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: An equation like $\log x + \log(x-3) = 1$ — the quadratic gives two roots.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Combine into one log, convert to power form, solve.
Reject roots with non-positive arguments.

example.solution:
$x(x-3) = 10$, so $x = 5$ or $x = -2$
$x = -2$ breaks the domain, so **x = 5**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: $|2x - 3| = 5$ style — a modulus equals a number.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Split into $+$ and $-$ cases (or use distance).
Both solutions usually count.

Write both sides with the same base.
Equate exponents and solve.

solvedExamples.shortcut: Translate each log to power language and add.
Solve $f(t) = 5$ directly: $2t + 3 = 5t - 5$ gives $t = 8/3$ — one line, no inverse needed.

solvedExamples.q: The minimum value of $f(x) = x^2 - 12x + 40$ is:
solvedExamples.shortcut: Complete the square: $(x-6)^2 + 4$ — the square is $\ge 0$, so the least value is **4**.

solvedExamples.q: The minimum value of $|x - 1| + |x - 7|$ for real $x$ is:
solvedExamples.solution:
The two pins are at $1$ and $7$.
The sum of distances is least between the pins, and equals the gap: $7 - 1 = 6$.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Subtract the pins: $|1 - 7| = 6$. Any $x$ from 1 to 7 gives it.

solvedExamples.solution:
Combine: $\log_2 \big(x(x-7)\big) = 3$, so $x(x-7) = 8$.
$x^2 - 7x - 8 = 0$, so $(x-8)(x+1) = 0$: $x = 8$ or $x = -1$.
$x = -1$ makes $\log_2(-1)$ undefined — reject.
Answer: $x = 8$. Check: $\log_2 8 + \log_2 1 = 3 + 0 = 3$. ✓
solvedExamples.shortcut: Reject any root with a non-positive argument — the trap option is always there.

On $x \ge 0$ the function is one-one, so the inverse exists.
$f^{-1}(81) = \sqrt{81} = 9$.

practice.shortcut: Jump in steps of 3: powers of the given value.

practice.solution: An outside $+4$ lifts every point by $4$: $y = x^2 + 4$.

practice.solution: An inside $-3$ works in reverse: the graph moves $3$ right.

$f(-x)$ mirrors in the $y$-axis: flip the sign of the $x$-coordinate.

practice.shortcut: Complete the square; read the constant.

The V with corner at $x = -2$ meets the line $y = 5$ twice.
Roots: $x = 3$ and $x = -7$.
practice.shortcut: Line above the corner: two crossings.

practice.solution:
$-f(x)$ mirrors in the $x$-axis: flip the sign of the $y$-coordinate.
$(3, 2)$.

practice.q: The quadratic $f(x) = x^2 + bx + 25$ has its minimum at $x = 4$. Then $b$ equals:
practice.solution:
Vertex input: $-b/2 = 4$, so $b = -8$.
Check: $f(4) = 16 - 32 + 25 = 9 > 0$, a genuine minimum.

practice.solution:
Corner at $x = 2.5$; the line $y = 3$ is above the corner.

practice.solution:
The V has corner $(1, 0)$; the line $y = 3$ sits above it.
Two crossings: $x = 4$ and $x = -2$.
practice.shortcut: Line above the corner: two meetings.

practice.shortcut: Shift the roots of $x^2 = 4$ right by 1.

Convert to power form, then check the argument.

practice.shortcut: Change of base: divide the two logs.

practice.q: The number of digits in $2^{64}$ is ($\log_{10} 2 = 0.3010$):

practice.solution:
$\log_{10}\big(x(x-3)\big) = 1$, so $x(x-3) = 10$.
$x^2 - 3x - 10 = 0$ gives $x = 5$ or $x = -2$.
$x = -2$ makes the argument negative — reject. Answer: $x = 5$.

Base $\dfrac{1}{2}$ lies between 0 and 1, so the sign flips.
$\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^3 = \dfrac{1}{8}$, and $x$ must stay positive: $0 < x < \dfrac{1}{8}$.

$\log_4 x = \dfrac{1}{2}\log_2 x$.
So $\dfrac{3}{2}\log_2 x = 3$, giving $\log_2 x = 2$ and $x = 4$.
Check: $2 + 1 = 3$. ✓

Base $2 > 1$: direction stays.
$x < 2^4 = 16$, and $x$ must stay positive: $0 < x < 16$.

Match the base, read the power.

practice.solution: Band of radius $4$ around $3$: from $3 - 4 = -1$ to $3 + 4 = 7$.

$2x - 1 \ge 5$ gives $x \ge 3$.
$2x - 1 \le -5$ gives $x \le -2$.
Two arms joined by 'or'.

Case $x \ge 3$: $x - 3 = 2x - 5$ gives $x = 2$ — rejected, it breaks the case.
Case $x < 3$: $3 - x = 2x - 5$ gives $x = \dfrac{8}{3}$.
Check: $\left|\dfrac{8}{3} - 3\right| = \dfrac{1}{3} = 2 \cdot \dfrac{8}{3} - 5$. ✓

practice.q: How many integers $x$ with $-5 \le x \le 5$ satisfy $|x - 1| < 3$?
practice.solution:
$-3 < x - 1 < 3$ gives $-2 < x < 4$.
Integers: $-1, 0, 1, 2, 3$ — five of them.

practice.q: The number of real solutions of $x^2 - 5|x| + 6 = 0$ is:
practice.solution:
Let $t = |x|$: $t^2 - 5t + 6 = 0$ gives $t = 2$ or $t = 3$.
Each gives two values of $x$: $\pm 2$, $\pm 3$ — four in all.

practice.q: The equation $|x - 1| = x + 3$ has the solution:
practice.solution:
Case $x \ge 1$: $x - 1 = x + 3$ gives $-1 = 3$ — impossible, no root here.
Case $x < 1$: $1 - x = x + 3$ gives $2x = -2$, so $x = -1$.
Check: $|-1 - 1| = 2$ and $-1 + 3 = 2$. ✓
Answer: $x = -1$ only.
practice.shortcut: One case can be impossible; always check the survivor.
